A CLEAR START. AN AGREED OUTCOME.

What is an AI workflow?

An AI workflow is an agreed sequence of steps that uses AI and connected software to move a business task forward. It defines what starts the process, which information is needed, what actions are allowed and when a person should approve or take over.

Start with one task your team repeats, such as handling a new enquiry or following up a booking request. We map the steps and confirm what can be supported by your information, tools and approval rules.

A clear starting point

Define the event that starts the work, such as a call or supported enquiry form. Agree on the details needed before the process can continue.

The next useful action

With the relevant tools connected, a workflow may save agreed information, prepare a message or give staff a follow-up task. Each action is confirmed in the scope.

Approval where it matters

Decide what can happen automatically and what needs review. Sensitive decisions, exceptions and actions outside the approved process go to your team.

A visible unfinished state

Agree what happens when information is missing or a connection fails. Staff should be able to distinguish a completed step from a request still waiting for attention.

START WITH ONE REPEATED TASK

How we shape your workflow.

A useful first workflow has a clear owner, a small number of agreed steps and a way to handle exceptions.

  1. 01

    Map the current process

    Show us a typical enquiry or task. Identify where staff repeat work, which details get lost and what a completed result should look like.

  2. 02

    Agree on actions and approvals

    Define the trigger, required information, allowed actions and human review points. Confirm who takes responsibility when a request falls outside the process.

  3. 03

    Check connections and test cases

    Review supported access to your tools. Test routine cases, missing details, duplicate requests and unavailable systems before enabling an action.

  4. 04

    Review before launch

    Walk through the outcome with your team. Agree how to see pending work, change rules and maintain the workflow as your business or software changes.

What to bring to the first conversation

  • One task or enquiry your team handles repeatedly.
  • The steps staff follow today and the tools they use.
  • A few fictional or appropriately redacted examples.
  • The decisions that need approval and a contact for exceptions.

PRACTICAL ANSWERS

Common questions about ai workflows.

How is an AI workflow different from ordinary automation?

A fixed rule can handle predictable steps, such as routing a completed form. AI can help interpret an enquiry or prepare a response where the task calls for it. A workflow may combine both approaches, with clear limits around what the AI may decide or change.

Can it work with the tools we already use?

We review your current software, plan permissions and supported connections. The exact fields and actions must be checked before an integration is included. Existing tools are the starting point; compatibility is confirmed during scoping.

Can a person approve a message or action first?

Yes, approval can be part of the workflow design. Agree which steps may proceed automatically and which need staff review before anything is sent, booked or updated. The available approval mechanism depends on the connected tools.

What happens if a workflow fails?

The fallback is agreed before launch. It may record a pending request, notify a team contact or pass the task to a person. Retry behaviour and duplicate prevention need to be checked for each connection. A failed step should not be described as successfully completed.

What customer information does it need?

Only the information required for the agreed task should be included. Define the fields, permitted uses, access and retention requirements when mapping the process. Avoid adding unrelated or unnecessary customer information to a workflow.

Do workflows have to start with a phone call?

No. A workflow can start from another supported event, such as an enquiry form or a change in a connected system. We check whether the chosen tool can provide the event and the information needed for the next step.

Who maintains the rules after launch?

Maintenance responsibilities are agreed in the scope. Identify who owns business information, approvals and software access, and how changes are requested and tested. A change to a connected service or business process may require the workflow to be reviewed.

How much does a workflow cost and how long does it take?

The scope depends on the number of steps, supported connections, data preparation, review requirements and testing. Software providers may charge separately. We review one use case before quoting and agreeing on delivery; no fixed price or timeline is published here.
